title: Jonah and the Typewriter
premise: In 1936, on a storm-battered Cornish headland, widowed lighthouse keeper Hazel Montrose finds an abandoned child clutching a typewritten page that could topple a shipping magnate whose fleet runs contraband under naval cover. The child, Jonah, cannot speak of where he came from, and the page is only half the evidence — the rest sits in the magnate's own house, where Hazel's late husband once worked. Over one brutal winter, Hazel and Jonah smuggle the documents past three checkpoints — the harbor watch, the magistrate's son, and finally the magnate himself — while the lighthouse, and their fragile bond, threaten to fail. In the end Hazel chooses to burn her husband's letters to save Jonah's future, testifying at the inquiry with nothing but her name, and discovers that belonging is not inherited but built, storm by storm.
about_author: Jude Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing coastal shipping records in Cornwall before turning to fiction. They write about ordinary people caught in the machinery of history, and live within earshot of the sea.

chapters.title: The Light Keeps Its Own Hours
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Establishes her isolated routine, grief for her drowned husband Edmund, and her conviction that history belongs to cities and parliaments, not to her rock. A violent storm forces her to keep the lamp burning all night alone. Emotional beat: loneliness worn like a uniform, pride in endurance masking emptiness.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. After the storm she finds seven-year-old Jonah asleep against her door, soaked, with a note: 'Forget the face' — and a typed page naming ships, dates, and cargo that make no sense until she recognizes her late husband's shorthand corrections in the margins. Emotional beat: fear curdling into reluctant responsibility; the first crack in her belief that history happens elsewhere.

chapters.title: What Edmund Left Behind
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV with a flashback chapter. She searches Edmund's old effects and learns he clerked for magnate Ambrose Vane before his death, and that his 'accident' may not have been one. Jonah begins to speak in fragments — a house, a cellar, a woman's voice. Emotional beat: grief reinterpreted as betrayal; suspicion replacing mourning.

chapters.title: The Harbor Watch
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. First checkpoint: to reach the mainland inquiry office she must pass the harbor, now watched by Vane's men posing as customs officers. She hides the page inside the lighthouse logbook and talks her way through using her keeper's authority. Emotional beat: terror managed through competence; the intoxicating discovery that she can lie well when it matters.

chapters.title: Jonah Speaks
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, the novel's first shift. He remembers the Vane household, the woman — Vane's secretary, who hid him and typed the page — and the night he was sent away. He trusts Hazel because she smells of lamp oil like his mother did. Emotional beat: a child's loyalty outlasting fear; Hazel realizing she is no longer keeping him, he is keeping her.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Son
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Second checkpoint: the local magistrate, whom she hoped would help, turns out to be Vane's debtor, and his son — a boy Jonah's age — nearly exposes them out of innocent curiosity. Hazel must decide whether to trust the son with the truth. Emotional beat: the cost of isolation revealed; trust offered as a calculated gamble that half-pays off.

chapters.title: Into the House of Vane
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Hazel infiltrates a Vane dinner party as contracted lamp-oil supplier while Jonah waits with the magistrate's son. She retrieves Edmund's hidden second set of ledgers from the cellar Jonah described — and comes face to face with Vane, who recognizes Edmund's name. Emotional beat: dread and defiance braided together; the past demanding its price.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, One Night
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Third and final checkpoint: Vane has sealed the roads and offers Hazel her husband's letters — proof of Edmund's complicity — in exchange for the ledgers and the child. Cornered during the worst storm of the year, she burns the letters in the lantern room rather than trade Jonah. Emotional beat: climax; grief finally chosen over leverage, power refused at personal ruin.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. With the ledgers delivered by the magistrate's son when the roads open, Hazel testifies in Truro with no corroborating papers of her own, only testimony and the logbook. Vane's empire cracks; the secretary surfaces to confirm everything. Emotional beat: exposure without armor; the quiet shock of being believed.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Light
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, spring. The inquiry ends, Vane is indicted, and Hazel formally petitions to adopt Jonah — not as Edmund's shadow or Vane's orphan, but as her own choice. The storms pass; the light still turns. Emotional beat: resolution; inheritance redefined as what we build together, and belonging earned one kept promise at a time.
